item.title: What You Actually Pulled: Reading Quantisation, Parameter Count and Context Out of an Ollama GGUF File
item.description: A 31B tag pulls 18.99 GiB of layers — an 18,670,033,120-byte model blob against 61.4 GB for the same weights in bf16 — and nothing ollama prints says which quantisation is inside. An 8–32 MiB ranged read of the GGUF header returns the tensor table, so bits per weight, parameter count and the declared context field become numbers you can check before the download finishes.
item.content:encoded:
You pulled a tag. The download is 18.99 GiB for a model the card calls 31B. The agent that needed long history behaves as if it had a fraction of the context the card advertises. The quality does not match the benchmark chart that made you choose the model in the first place. None of those three surprises is a property of the model. All three are properties of the artifact: which quantisation the tag actually resolved to, how many bits per weight that quantisation really costs, and which metadata value declares the context this particular build was made for.

This article answers those three questions from the bytes rather than from the tag name. Every figure below comes from a ranged HTTP read of the file header — 8 to 32 MiB out of a 5–19 GB file — so no weights were downloaded, no server was started, and no throughput, quality or VRAM claim is made or implied. Five artifacts were read on 2026-11-06: three published GGUF files and two Ollama registry blobs.

The file on disk does not match the card

The unsloth repository unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-GGUF lists its bf16 build as two shards of 49,950,156,960 and 11,463,033,568 bytes, which is 61,413,190,528 bytes or 57.2 GiB (repository index). The same index lists gemma-4-31B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf at 18,323,733,440 bytes. That is 17.07 GiB, 18.32 decimal GB, and 3.35× smaller than the bf16 build.

So “18 GB, not 48 GB” contains two separate confusions. The 18 figure is real: it is the 4-bit file, and it looks smaller in GiB than in decimal GB because binary units divide by 1,073,741,824. The 48 figure corresponds to nothing in that repository — the bf16 weights there are 61.41 decimal GB, and a Q8_0 build of the same weights lands at 8.5 bits per weight rather than 16. Once the quantisation is known, both sizes are arithmetic.

The catch is that 31B is a name, not a specification. The name tells you the parameter class; it says nothing about the 4.77 bits per weight the file actually spends. ollama show prints a Modelfile back at you, and that Modelfile is a description of how to load the blob, not of what is inside it. The manifest audit in the tag-size article takes the first step: it divides a manifest’s model-layer bytes by the parameter total published by the model repository, and states plainly that it did not inspect tensors. This piece takes the second step and reads the tensor table, so numerator and denominator come from the same file.

GGUF is a directory inside a file

A GGUF file begins with the magic GGUF, a version, a tensor count and a metadata key/value count, then a metadata block of typed key/value pairs, then one tensor-info record per tensor holding its name, dimensions, quantisation type and byte offset. The weight data starts after that array, padded to the alignment boundary, and each tensor offset is relative to the start of the data section rather than to the start of the file (GGUF specification).

That layout is what makes a header read sufficient. The tensor-info array carries the type of every tensor and the size of every dimension, so the full weight map — how many bytes at which precision, how many elements in total — is available before a single weight is fetched. The weights themselves are only needed to run the model, not to describe it.

Reading it without downloading it

The probe sends two requests per artifact. A HEAD gives Content-Length, the exact size of the file. A GET with Range: bytes=0-33554431 returns the first 32 MiB, which is enough for the metadata block, the tokenizer arrays and the tensor-info array of a 262,144-token vocabulary.

The window has to clear the header, and how much that takes is a property of the file, not a constant. A 1 MiB window fails on the Gemma file before the tensor table is complete (EOFError: window ended at 1048576; need 13 more), and 8 MiB still fails there (window ended at 8388608; need 8 more) because the 262,144-token vocabulary pushes the weight section out to byte 15,834,176. The same 8 MiB window was already enough for both Qwen3 files, whose weight sections start at 5,956,416 and 5,956,384 bytes. In the saved batch three artifacts parsed at 32 MiB — the Gemma file and both registry blobs — and two parsed at 8 MiB (Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M at 14:34:01Z, Qwen3-8B-Q8_0 at 14:34:04Z); a later 32 MiB rerun of Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M at 14:41:15Z reproduced the same values. The parser raises on a short window instead of returning the tensors it managed to read, which matters: a silently truncated tensor list still produces a plausible-looking bits-per-weight number that is simply wrong.

The five successful reads ran between 14:34:01Z and 14:34:33Z on 2026-11-06, each returning HTTP 206 and taking 1.41–4.03 s of wall clock. The two registry blobs answered fastest (1.41 s and 1.62 s) and the Gemma file slowest (4.03 s), a spread that tracks the origin rather than the 8- or 32-MiB span. The SHA-256 of each fetched span was recorded so a later rerun can prove it read the same bytes.

Worked example: gemma-4-31B-it Q4_K_M

The file’s header declares architecture gemma4, 60 blocks, 262,144 tokens of context, and 833 tensors. Adding up the dimensions gives 30,697,345,596 stored elements — the parameter count of this file, not of the family. Multiplying each tensor’s element count by its type’s block width gives 18,307,897,584 bytes of weights.

Quantisation Tensors Bytes Share of weight bytes
Q4_K (4.5 bpw nominal) 356 15,006,007,296 81.96%
Q6_K (6.5625 bpw nominal) 55 3,296,563,200 18.01%
F32 (32 bpw) 422 5,327,088 0.03%

8 × 18,307,897,584 ÷ 30,697,345,596 = 4.7712 bits per weight. The 422 F32 tensors are almost all small norms and biases: they are 422 of the 833 tensor records but 0.03% of the bytes.

The reconciliation is what makes that ratio trustworthy rather than decorative. The weight section begins at byte 15,834,176, so the file’s published size leaves 18,307,899,264 bytes for weights. The tensor table accounts for 18,307,897,584 of them — a residue of 1,680 bytes, 0.00001%, which is the alignment padding after the final tensor. A wrong block table, a missed tensor or a misread dimension cannot land on that total by accident.

Why “4-bit” is 4.77 and “8-bit” is 8.50

Block geometry explains the gap between the label and the measurement. In llama.cpp’s quantisation table a K-quant block covers 256 elements: Q4_K spends 144 bytes per block (4.5 bpw), Q6_K spends 210 (6.5625 bpw), and Q8_0 — a 32-element block — spends 34 (8.5 bpw) (constants.py).

A Q4_K_M file is a mixture. The _M variant keeps selected tensors at a higher precision, so on the Gemma file 18.01% of weight bytes are Q6_K and the blended figure is 4.7712 rather than 4.5. The Qwen3-8B Q4_K_M file shows the same mechanism at a different ratio: 3,704,979,456 bytes of Q4_K, 1,315,614,720 of Q6_K and 1,232,896 of F32 over 8,190,735,360 elements, giving 4.9049 bpw with 26.20% of weight bytes at Q6_K. The Q8_0 build of the same 8.19B parameters spends 8,702,328,832 bytes at Q8_0 plus the same 1,232,896 bytes of F32 and measures 8.5009.

The practical consequence: “4-bit” and “8-bit” are labels for a mixture, and the blended figure moves with how much of the file the quantizer kept at higher precision. If the number matters — and it does when you are deciding whether a file fits in VRAM or on a laptop disk — it has to be summed from the tensors.

The tag is not the file

An Ollama tag resolves to a registry manifest, and that manifest names layers with exact byte sizes and digests. Reading the model layer of gemma4:31b and parsing it the same way gives a different file from the same-named Hugging Face build.

Artifact Bytes Q4_K bytes Q6_K bytes Parameters bpw
HF gemma-4-31B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf 18,323,733,440 15,006,007,296 3,296,563,200 30,697,345,596 4.7712
Ollama gemma4:31b model layer 18,670,033,120 14,250,442,752 4,398,428,160 30,697,345,596 4.8614

Same architecture, same 60 blocks, same 262,144-token context field, same parameter count — 346,299,680 more bytes, and a different mixture: 23.58% of the tag’s weight bytes are Q6_K against 18.01% in the Hugging Face file. The manifest’s own from field names the upstream publisher tag dhiltgen/gemma4:31b-it-mtp-q4_K_M-llamacpp, not a Hugging Face repository, so size and mixture similarity cannot establish which repository this blob was converted from. Treat provenance as unknown and check the bytes you have.

The same divergence appears at 8B. The Ollama qwen3:8b model layer is 5,225,374,496 bytes against 5,027,783,488 for Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M.gguf, and it carries 301,989,888 bytes of F16 tensors the Hugging Face Q4_K_M does not, with 1,253,683,200 bytes of Q6_K against 1,315,614,720. Bits per weight: 5.0979 versus 4.9049, over an identical 8,190,735,360 parameters.

A tag can also be more than one model. gemma4:31b is projector 1,200,726,368 + model 18,670,033,120 + draft 514,687,072 bytes — 20,385,446,560 weight-bearing bytes, and 20,385,457,992 bytes across every layer including template, license and params. That is 18.99 GiB of download for a file advertised as 31B at 4-bit. The projector is a separate artifact with its own cost profile, covered in the projector article; it is not part of a weights-only bits-per-weight ratio, and adding it to the denominator would make the number meaningless.

Which context value wins

Three different quantities get called “the context length”, and they are not interchangeable.

The first is the field inside the artifact. Parsing the metadata block gives gemma4.context_length = 262144 and qwen3.context_length = 40960. For the Qwen3-8B files that 40,960 is the positional-embedding allocation the vendor ships in config.json as max_position_embeddings; it is not a statement of the length the weights were trained on.

The second is the model card’s own framing, which states the limits separately: “Context Length: 32,768 natively and 131,072 tokens with YaRN”. The card then explains where 40,960 comes from: “The default max_position_embeddings in config.json is set to 40,960. This allocation includes reserving 32,768 tokens for outputs and 8,192 tokens for typical prompts, which is sufficient for most scenarios involving short text processing” (Qwen3-8B card). Read as three numbers rather than one: 32,768 native, 131,072 with YaRN scaling, and 40,960 as a padded default that splits into an 8,192-token prompt budget and 32,768 reserved for generation. An agent carrying a 30k-token tool history is asking for more prompt than that arrangement allows, on a card whose headline number reads “40,960”.

The third is the runtime option, and it is the one that decides what is actually served. Ollama’s Modelfile reference defines PARAMETER num_ctx 4096 as setting “the context window size to 4096, this controls how many tokens the LLM can use as context to generate the next token” (Modelfile reference), and a tag’s params layer is where such a value would be baked in. Both tags’ params layers are readable: the registry blob URL answers HTTP 307 to a presigned object URL, and following it returns 64 bytes for gemma4:31b (draft_num_predict, temperature, top_k, top_p) and 120 bytes for qwen3:8b (repeat_penalty, stop, temperature, top_k, top_p). Neither contains num_ctx, so neither tag pins a window. What is established is the boundary: the artifact’s declared length is not the served length, the tag’s params do not set it, and the value that does comes from a server default or a per-request option. The truncation diagnosis covers what the server does when a conversation exceeds that cap.

A five-minute checklist before trusting a tag

  1. Run ollama show --modelfile qwen3:8b and read the PARAMETER lines and the architecture line. That is the loading recipe, not the file contents.
  2. Take the file’s exact size: curl -sI <resolve-url> | grep -i content-length, or read the model layer’s size from the registry manifest at https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/<family>/manifests/<tag>.
  3. Compare that size with the size the same-named file has in the model repository. A mismatch means the tag is a different requantisation, which is normal, not a bug — but it means benchmarks measured on the repository file do not automatically describe your file.
  4. Fetch the first 32 MiB and parse the header with the script below. You get the quantisation mix, the parameter count, the declared context and the bits per weight in one pass.
  5. Sanity-check the ratio against block geometry: a Q4_K_M file at 7B or larger typically blends to the high 4s, and anything inside 4.5–5.2 is a normal mixture; a Q8_0 file lands near 8.5. A figure outside that band means the parser or the fixture is wrong.
  6. Read context_length from the same output and set num_ctx deliberately. Do not inherit a default and then debug the model’s memory.

What this check cannot tell you

The measurement is a weights-only ratio: metadata, tokenizer arrays and alignment padding are excluded by construction, which is why the reconciliation compares against Content-Length minus the data offset rather than the whole file. It says nothing about output quality, tokens per second, VRAM in use or whether the mixture is a good one — all of those need a running server and a workload, and none was measured here. It covers five artifacts: three published GGUF files and two registry blobs, with no IQ-series, Q3, Q5 or MXFP4 file parsed. Ollama tags are mutable, so every size and digest here is true for 2026-11-06 and can change when a tag is re-pushed. And the ratio cannot prove where a blob came from; it can only prove what is inside the bytes you fetched.

Reproduce it

Save this as probe_range.py and run python3 probe_range.py <gguf-url>. It downloads no weights, needs no account, and prints one JSON record per artifact.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Read a GGUF header over HTTP Range: quant mix, bits-per-weight, parameters, context."""
import json
import struct
import sys
import urllib.request

# (elements_per_block, bytes_per_block) from llama.cpp gguf-py/gguf/constants.py
BLOCK = {"F32": (1, 4), "F16": (1, 2), "BF16": (1, 2), "Q4_0": (32, 18), "Q4_1": (32, 20),
         "Q5_0": (32, 22), "Q5_1": (32, 24), "Q8_0": (32, 34), "Q2_K": (256, 84),
         "Q3_K": (256, 110), "Q4_K": (256, 144), "Q5_K": (256, 176), "Q6_K": (256, 210),
         "Q8_K": (256, 292)}
SCALAR = {0: "B", 1: "b", 2: "H", 3: "h", 4: "I", 5: "i", 6: "f", 7: "?",
          10: "Q", 11: "q", 12: "d"}
ENUM = {0: "F32", 1: "F16", 2: "Q4_0", 3: "Q4_1", 4: "Q4_1", 5: "Q5_0", 6: "Q5_0",
        7: "Q5_1", 8: "Q8_0", 9: "Q8_1", 10: "Q2_K", 11: "Q3_K", 12: "Q4_K",
        13: "Q5_K", 14: "Q6_K", 15: "Q8_K", 30: "BF16"}


class Reader:
    def __init__(self, buf):
        self.b, self.p = buf, 0

    def take(self, n):
        if self.p + n > len(self.b):
            raise EOFError(f"window ended at {len(self.b)}; need {n} more")
        out = self.b[self.p:self.p + n]
        self.p += n
        return out

    def scalar(self, fmt):
        return struct.unpack("<" + fmt, self.take(struct.calcsize(fmt)))[0]

    def string(self):
        return self.take(self.scalar("Q")).decode("utf-8", "replace")

    def skip_value(self, vtype):
        if vtype in SCALAR:
            self.take(struct.calcsize(SCALAR[vtype]))
        elif vtype == 8:
            self.take(self.scalar("Q"))
        elif vtype == 9:
            inner, count = self.scalar("I"), self.scalar("Q")
            for _ in range(count):
                self.skip_value(inner)
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown metadata value type {vtype}")


def probe(url, span=32 * 1024 * 1024):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"Range": f"bytes=0-{span - 1}",
                                              "User-Agent": "gguf-range-probe/1.0"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60) as resp:
        buf, status = resp.read(), resp.status
        length = int(resp.headers["Content-Range"].rsplit("/", 1)[1])
    r = Reader(buf)
    if r.take(4) != b"GGUF":
        raise ValueError("not a GGUF file")
    version, n_tensors, n_kv = r.scalar("I"), r.scalar("Q"), r.scalar("Q")
    meta = {}
    for _ in range(n_kv):
        key = r.string()
        if SCALAR.get((vtype := r.scalar("I"))):
            meta[key] = r.scalar(SCALAR[vtype])
        elif vtype == 8:
            meta[key] = r.string()
        else:
            r.skip_value(vtype)
    tensors = []
    for _ in range(n_tensors):
        name = r.string()
        dims = [r.scalar("Q") for _ in range(r.scalar("I"))]
        tensors.append((name, dims, ENUM.get(r.scalar("I"), "?"), r.scalar("Q")))
    data_start = (r.p + 31) // 32 * 32
    mix, elements, nbytes = {}, 0, 0
    for _name, dims, qtype, _off in tensors:
        count = 1
        for d in dims:
            count *= d
        if qtype not in BLOCK:
            raise ValueError(f"block table missing {qtype}")
        per, width = BLOCK[qtype]
        size = count // per * width
        mix[qtype] = mix.get(qtype, 0) + size
        elements += count
        nbytes += size
    arch = meta.get("general.architecture", "?")
    return {"url": url, "http_status": status, "content_length": length,
            "range_bytes": len(buf), "gguf_version": version,
            "architecture": arch, "file_type": meta.get("general.file_type"),
            "context_length": meta.get(f"{arch}.context_length"),
            "block_count": meta.get(f"{arch}.block_count"),
            "parameter_count": elements, "weight_bytes": nbytes,
            "bits_per_weight": round(8 * nbytes / elements, 4),
            "quant_mix_bytes": dict(sorted(mix.items())),
            "tensor_count": n_tensors, "header_data_start": data_start,
            "weight_section_bytes": length - data_start}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(probe(sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 32 << 20), indent=1))

Run against the Gemma file, the script prints content_length: 18323733440, parameter_count: 30697345596, bits_per_weight: 4.7712, header_data_start: 15834176 and the three-entry quantisation mix — the figures in the table above, reproduced from a fresh ranged read on 2026-11-06 at 14:41Z.

The run records behind those numbers — the probe output, the window-failure records, the registry manifests, the two params-layer bodies, the fetched spec and the method note — are kept in this article’s evidence directory under research/evidence/ollama-gguf-artifact-forensics-2026/ as a private author-side verification set, hashed in the review receipt so each figure can be re-checked against what was actually fetched. They are not offered as a downloadable dataset, and no reader-facing archive is promised; the script above regenerates every row on your machine.

Sources

  • GGUF file format specification, ggml-org/ggml: https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md
  • Ollama Modelfile reference (PARAMETER num_ctx): https://docs.ollama.com/modelfile.md
  • unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-GGUF file index with per-file sizes and SHA-256: https://huggingface.co/api/models/unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-GGUF?blobs=true
  • Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF file index: https://huggingface.co/api/models/Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF?blobs=true
  • Ollama registry manifest for gemma4:31b: https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/gemma4/manifests/31b
  • Ollama registry manifest for qwen3:8b: https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/qwen3/manifests/8b
  • Ollama gemma4:31b params layer (64 B, follows a 307 to object storage): https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/gemma4/blobs/sha256:2365fbb6d97bf654fdda0353b7505baa2254c662122cff0f153e4b47e6220ded
  • Ollama qwen3:8b params layer (120 B, follows a 307 to object storage): https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/qwen3/blobs/sha256:cff3f395ef3756ab63e58b0ad1b32bb6f802905cae1472e6a12034e4246fbbdb
  • Qwen3-8B model card (40,960-token allocation): https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B
  • llama.cpp quantisation block sizes, gguf-py/gguf/constants.py: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/master/gguf-py/gguf/constants.py

item.title: The Tag Says Nothing About Bits: Reading a Local Model's Real Quantization From Its Registry Manifest
item.description: Pull a 32B model, get an 18-20 GB file, and nothing on the tag says why. Sum the manifest's weight layer, divide by the model's own parameter count, and the quantization becomes a number you can check before downloading.
item.content:encoded:
You ran ollama pull qwen3:32b. The progress bar stopped somewhere between 18 GB and 20 GB, the model answered, and nothing in the output told you what you had just downloaded. A 32-billion-parameter model needs 64 GB at bf16. You got a fifth of that. The tag said 32b and stopped there: no q4_K_M, no q8_0, no indication that four bits per weight is what your download actually contains.

That gap is measurable before you download a single byte. An Ollama tag resolves to a registry manifest that lists each layer with its exact byte size, and the manifest’s config blob carries the field the tag name omits. This article does that arithmetic on 14 tags across 7 model families and shows the numbers, the fetch times, and the code to reproduce them.

The download that looks broken

For qwen3:32b, the weights layer in the manifest is 20,201,240,160 bytes. That single number explains the whole confusion:

  • 20,201,240,160 bytes = 20.201 decimal GB (the figure a registry page, a download counter or a package listing reports)
  • 20,201,240,160 bytes = 18.814 GiB (the same bytes in binary units — the “18.8 GB” that appears in blog posts and in tools that print GiB)

Both figures describe the same artifact, and which one a given tool prints is a formatting choice, not a different file. Nobody truncated the download and nobody shipped you a 2 GB shard of a 64 GB model. A 32B model at four bits per weight is supposed to be about 20 GB, and that is exactly what arrives. The “18 GB vs 48 GB” question that sends people to a search box is a unit mismatch layered on top of an unstated quantization level.

The manifest for that tag was fetched at 2026-11-03T00:22:45Z and its bytes hash to 030ee887880fc378860c2dd35101da424377520441ae4bfe7be6deff8ade7840. Every number below is bound to a digest like that one, because registry tags can be re-pointed even though the blobs behind a digest are immutable.

What the tag promises, and what the manifest proves

A tag name is a label, not a contract. qwen3:32b names a family and a size. qwen3:32b-q8_0 names a family, a size and a quantization. mistral:7b names a family and a size while the file it points at is 4-bit. The manifest is where the file becomes specific:

  1. config.digest — points at a small JSON blob. That blob has a file_type field. For qwen3:32b it reads Q4_K_M; the config blob itself is a digest-addressed read of 488 bytes.
  2. layers[] — each entry has mediaType and size. The weights are the layer with mediaType: application/vnd.ollama.image.model, and that layer alone is what the bits-per-weight arithmetic divides: it is the file that holds the tensors the quantization applies to.
  3. The other layers are separate downloads with other jobs: template, params and license are metadata, and a multimodal tag adds application/vnd.ollama.image.projector. The metadata layers are small — 1,723 bytes of template, 11,338 of license and 120 of params on qwen3:32b, about 13 KB in total — but the projector is not: on gemma3:4b it is 851,251,104 bytes, another 34% on top of the 2,499,012,288-byte weight layer. So the pull is 3,350,272,259 bytes even though the weights are 2.5 GB. The projector is part of the download and not part of the bpw calculation; the two numbers answer different questions, and a table that shows only one of them is wrong about the other.
  4. The layer digest — a second, independent fingerprint of the weights you are about to pull.

So one unauthenticated GET to the manifest, one to the config blob, decides which weights are being served. No key, no auth, no blob download: the 47 reads behind this article’s table spanned 18.14 seconds of wall clock, which is under a second for the manifest-plus-config pair of a single tag on this host.

Method: weight bytes × 8 ÷ parameter count

Bits per weight is a size accounting, and it only needs two honest inputs:

  • Weight bytes from the manifest’s model layer, as above.
  • Parameter count from the model repository’s own metadata — the safetensors.total field in Hugging Face’s /api/models/<repo> response for the exact repository that model card names. Never estimated from file size, because that would make the whole calculation circular.

The nominal figures the measurement is compared against come from llama.cpp’s own block definitions in gguf-py/gguf/constants.py, not from a vendor’s marketing page: a Q4_K block is 144 bytes per 256 weights (4.5 bpw), Q6_K is 210 bytes per 256 weights (6.5625 bpw), Q8_0 is 34 bytes per 32 weights (8.5 bpw). A Q4_K_M file is a mixed layout that keeps some tensors at Q6_K, which puts a healthy file at roughly 4.85 bpw overall.

That gives a reconciliation test anyone can apply: if weights_bytes × 8 ÷ parameters lands within ±3% of the nominal bpw for the quant the config blob claims, the manifest arithmetic is trustworthy and the download is what it says it is. If it lands wildly off, either the parameter count is wrong or the file is not what the tag claims.

The audit: 14 tags, 7 families

Each tag links to the manifest it was measured from. file_type is read from that manifest’s config blob, not guessed from the tag name. Fetch window: 2026-11-03T00:22:44Z to 00:22:50Z, all HTTP 200.

The last column is what ollama pull actually transfers: weights plus every other layer in that manifest, summed from the same saved bytes. For the eleven tags without a projector layer it differs from the weights by at most 14 KB and can be ignored. For the three gemma3 tags it does not: 851 MB, 854 MB and 858 MB of projector ride along, which is why gemma3:4b costs 3.350 GB of disk and not 2.499 GB.

Tag file_type (from config) Weight bytes Decimal GB GiB Measured bpw vs nominal All-layer pull (bytes / decimal GB)
qwen3:4b Q4_K_M 2,497,280,480 2.497 2.326 4.967 +2.41% 2,497,293,444 / 2.497
qwen3:8b Q4_K_M 5,225,374,496 5.225 4.867 5.104 +5.23% 5,225,387,677 / 5.225

Ten of fourteen tags land inside ±3%. The four that do not are not broken downloads, and understanding why is the difference between a measurement and a superstition:

  • gemma3:4b at 4.649 bpw (-4.14%) is smaller per weight than a textbook Q4_K_M, using the repository total of 4,300,079,472 parameters. A blended figure below 4.85 means part of that model carries fewer bits per weight than the Q4_K_M nominal, on average; which tensors, this audit does not identify. The 851 MB projector layer on this tag is not part of the divisor — it is a separate download — and whether the published parameter total counts parameters that live in that layer is not something this audit established.
  • qwen3:8b (+5.23%) and deepseek-r1:8b (+7.33%) are larger per weight. Both are 8B-class models, where the token embedding and output projection are a big fraction of all parameters and are commonly kept at higher precision than the transformer blocks, which pushes the blended figure up. I did not inspect these files tensor by tensor, so treat that as the expected mechanism rather than a proven per-tensor result.
  • qwen2.5:0.5b at 6.442 bpw (+32.82%) is the clearest case: at 494,032,768 parameters the embedding and output matrices are a large share of the model, so any precision kept on them dominates the blended number. A small model is exactly where the average diverges most from the block nominal.

The practical reading: bpw is a range per quant, not a constant. For Q4_K_M in this sample it spans 4.649 to 6.442, and a ±3% test on a model under 1B parameters will produce false alarms. The test tells you whether a download is plausible, not whether every tensor is where you think it is.

One model, two quantizations, one comparison

Because parameter count is fixed per model, two tags of the same family compare directly on manifest bytes. qwen3:32b and qwen3:32b-q8_0 both report 32,762,123,264 parameters. Weights go from 20,201,240,160 bytes to 35,132,291,680 bytes — a factor of 1.739 — and bpw from 4.933 to 8.579. That is the entire trade: you get more precision and pay 74% more disk and, at inference, more memory bandwidth per token. Whether Q8_0 is worth it for your workload is a quality question this audit does not answer.

The same table also settles a claim worth testing rather than repeating: the served quant is a property of the tag, not of your VRAM. qwen3:32b is Q4_K_M because the tag points at a Q4_K_M manifest, and ollama pull qwen3:32b will pull those exact bytes on a 12 GB laptop and on a 96 GB workstation alike. Ollama chooses between tags you name; it does not silently rebuild a different quant of the tag you asked for.

Run it yourself

The reader script below is the compact form of the audit: it takes family:tag pairs, reads the manifest and its config blob, and prints weight bytes in both unit systems, the config’s file_type, the origin server’s own Date header, and a UTC timestamp taken after the body was read — never a hand-written time. It downloads no model blobs and needs no account.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""One-shot manifest audit: weights bytes -> bits per weight, no blob download."""
import hashlib, json, sys, urllib.request
from datetime import datetime, timezone

def get(url):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "manifest-audit/1.0"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as r:
        body = r.read()
        return body, r.status, r.headers.get("Date"), datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

def manifest(family, tag):
    body, status, server_date, read_at = get(
        f"https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/{family}/manifests/{tag}")
    m = json.loads(body)
    weights = sum(l["size"] for l in m["layers"]
                  if l["mediaType"] == "application/vnd.ollama.image.model")
    cfg, _, _, _ = get(f"https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/{family}/blobs/{m['config']['digest']}")
    return {"tag": f"{family}:{tag}", "http_status": status, "server_date": server_date,
            "read_at_utc": read_at, "manifest_sha256": hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest(),
            "weights_bytes": weights, "gb": round(weights / 1e9, 3),
            "gib": round(weights / 2**30, 3), "config_file_type": json.loads(cfg).get("file_type")}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for spec in sys.argv[1:]:
        family, tag = spec.split(":", 1)
        print(json.dumps(manifest(family, tag)))

Run python3 manifest_audit.py qwen3:32b phi4:14b and you get back the same manifest hash this article records (030ee887... for qwen3:32b, ac896e5b... for phi4:14b), which is how you verify the tag has not been re-pointed since 2026-11-03. To get bits per weight, divide: weights_bytes * 8 / parameters, with the parameter total taken from the model repository’s own metadata. Environment for this run: ollama version is 0.20.3 on a 2 vCPU / 11 GB Linux host; the 47 reads behind the table took about 18 seconds of wall clock and downloaded no weights.

Everything above was computed from saved response bytes: raw manifests, config blobs, model-repository metadata and the llama.cpp constant table are kept in this article’s evidence directory as a private author-side verification set, hashed in the review receipt so the numbers can be re-checked against what was actually fetched. They are not offered as a downloadable dataset — the script above regenerates the same rows on your machine, which is the more useful artifact anyway.

What this does not tell you

  • bpw is not quality. It is bytes per parameter. Two files at 4.9 bpw can differ in how badly they were quantized — which tensors were kept at higher precision, and with what calibration data. A perplexity or eval claim needs an eval, not this arithmetic.
  • Tags move. These numbers are scoped to the digests and fetch times recorded above. A re-pointed tag will produce different bytes and a different hash; run the script rather than trusting a table, including this one.
  • 14 tags is a sample, not a census. Seven families, chosen to include one model at two quants and one model small enough to check against a local pull. Do not generalize the deviation figures to the whole library.
  • One row was cross-checked locally. qwen2.5:0.5b was compared against the local blob store and ollama list on 2026-11-02: the weights digest and size matched the registry. The other 13 tags were never downloaded on this host.

If your download came out at 18.something GB for a 32B model, nothing is wrong. Read the config’s file_type, multiply the weight bytes by 8, divide by the parameter count, and you will know which weights you are running before the first token is generated.
